title: QSCOUT's Qubit-Boson Gate Set
authors: Edward C. Tortorici, Ethan C. McGarrigle, Brian K. McFarland, Wes L. Johnson, Daniel S. Lobser, Melissa C. Revelle, Brandon P. Ruzic, Susan M. Clark, Christopher G. Yale
abstract: The Quantum Scientific Computing Open User Testbed (QSCOUT) has developed a qubit-boson gate set for hybrid continuous-discrete variable (CV-DV) quantum computing. This document outlines how to utilize these gates on QSCOUT using Just Another Quantum Assembly Language, Jaqal\textsuperscript{TM}.
summary: This paper describes the operational framework for performing hybrid continuous-discrete variable quantum computation on the QSCOUT trapped-ion system. It details how to use specific laser pulse sequences and a custom language, Jaqal, to implement advanced gates like Conditional Beamsplitter and Squeeze. The work is crucial for advancing hardware realization by providing rigorous protocols for gate execution and state verification.
main_problem: The paper details how to implement a comprehensive qubit-boson gate set for hybrid continuous-discrete variable (CV-DV) quantum computation on the QSCOUT platform.
main_result: It provides specific pulse sequences and language commands (Jaqal) necessary to execute advanced gates like Conditional Beamsplitter and Conditional Squeeze, alongside methods for state preparation and measurement.
method: The implementation relies on precisely timed laser pulses driving resonant sidebands (JC/AJC) and utilizing four-tone interactions to engineer complex quantum operations.
model_or_system: The system is a trapped-ion quantum processor (QSCOUT) using Yb-171 ions, where qubits are encoded in internal spin states ($\sigma$) and motional modes ($a, a^\dagger$) act as bosonic degrees of freedom. The coupling allows for hybrid CV-DV operations.
key_observables: Fock state occupation probabilities ($p_n$), the characteristic function $\chi( eta)$, and the Wigner representation $W(\gamma)$ are key diagnostic tools used to verify gate fidelity and characterize motional states.
important_parameters: Gate parameters include rotation angles ($	heta$) and phases ($\phi$); squeezing is controlled by the complex parameter $\zeta$; detunings ($\Delta\omega, \delta$) govern sideband resonance.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that motional modes can be truncated in the Fock basis (e.g., $|n=10angle$), and state preparation relies on controlled sequential application of specific pulse sequences.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate fitting beating oscillations from AJC gates to extract Fock occupancies, and show circuits for probing $\chi( eta)$ using conditional displacement gates, alongside examples of tomography data.
paper_structure: The paper systematically introduces the platform (QSCOUT), defines fundamental gates (JC, AJC, CD, CR), details advanced gate implementations (BS, Squeeze) via specific Hamiltonians and pulse sequences, and concludes with measurement protocols for state characterization.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it bridges theoretical quantum control techniques (Hamiltonian engineering) directly to a physical hardware platform (trapped ions), providing actionable recipes for implementing complex quantum circuits in the CV-DV regime.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The flavors of radial modes for 6 ions labeled by mode index. Mode 0, the highest energy mode within a manifold, is the center of mass (COM) mode, and mode 1 is the the tilt mode. We refer to mode 2 as the drum mode, and the lowest energy mode (N −1) as the zig-zag mode (The remaining modes do not have strong naming conventions as they become more zig-zag-like in nature as the mode number increases). The qubits/ions are indexed starting from the center ion: they are labeled with increasing qubit number, alternating outward from the center, as seen on the left.

Figure 2: The radial confinement is elliptical, so that the two radial modes of the same mode index have different energies, such that ω0,i > ω1,j for all i and all j, where i is the mode index for the upper manifold and j is the mode index for the lower manifold. The two beams driving Raman transitions are orthogonal to the axial direction, so they only project onto the radial modes.

Figure 3: Motional sideband spectrum for 5 ions. The 5 flavors of radial modes each appear twice: one at a lower frequency (manifold = 1), and one at a higher frequency (manifold = 0). A qumode is then called out by specifying both a manifold and a mode index. The axial frequency manifold does not appear because the lasers do not project onto these modes.
